notes: West leads the ♠6 against 3NT.

It seems natural to finesse in dummy on West's spade lead. There is a great danger in making this play, however. East may win and switch to hearts. The defense will be able to knock out the ♥A before the clubs can be unblocked.
South can make certain of 9 tricks by rising with the ♠A at trick 1. South can unblock the clubs and cross to dummy in hearts.
Nine tricks are now easy, the ♠A, the ♥A, the ♦A, and 6 club tricks.

review.hl: NCQ NCJ NCT NC9 NC8 NC7 SCA SCK
NCQ NCJ NCT NC9 NC8 NC7 SCA SCK

notes: West leads the ♠J against 6NT. The opening lead is won by East with ♠A. East returns a spade, won by South. There are only 10 top tricks (1 spade, 3 hearts, 2 diamonds, and 4 clubs). The diamond suit is the only possible source of 2 extra tricks.

The ♦Q is missing and South can play either defender for that card. If diamonds are 3-3, South will be able to run the diamonds as long as he finds the ♦Q. If West has that card, it will be necessary to lead low to the ♦J on the first round of the suit.
If East has the ♦Q, South will have to rise with the ♦A and pass the ♦J through East. This plan will also work if East has a singleton ♦Q (if West has a singleton ♦Q, South cannot go wrong).

If West has a doubleton ♦Q, South can also succeed by playing low to the ♦J on the first round of the suit. If East has a doubleton ♦Q, South cannot succeed. Even if South rises with the ♦A, the ♦J will be covered. South will be held to 3 diamond tricks and West will be left with a certain stopper.

If either West or East has 4 or more diamonds to the ♦Q, the contract will have no hope. As doubleton ♦Q with West is more likely than singleton ♦Q with East, it is correct to play the ♦J from dummy on the first round of the suit.

There are 8 top tricks (3 spades, the ♥A, the ♦A, and 3 clubs). If West has the ♦K, it will be possible to make several overtricks by finessing in that suit. South should limit his aspirations to 9 tricks and concentrate on simply making his contract.
If either spades or clubs divide 3-3 a ninth trick will be available without risking the diamond finesse.
After winning the heart lead, South should begin by cashing the top honours in spades and clubs. When neither of these suits divide favourably, South must fall back on the diamond finesse.

notes: West leads the ♠Q against 6♥. This hand is all about where to win West's spade opening lead. South's club loser can eventually be discarded on dummy's diamonds. It appears that only the ♥A must be lost.

If South wins the opening lead in the closed hand, he will go down on the above lie of the cards. West will duck the first trump lead and win the next round. West will then place the lead in the dummy. South will be unable to get off of the dummy to draw West's remaining trumps. If South tries to play diamonds, West will be able to ruff the second round.

If South wins the opening lead with the ♠A in dummy, the contract is safe. West will win the second round of hearts as before, but South will have maintained a spade entry to his hand so that West's remaining trumps can be drawn.

review.hl: NDA NDK NDQ NDJ NDT ND9
NDA NDK NDQ NDJ NDT ND9

notes: West leads the ♥J against 6♠. West's lead should be won in dummy. South's only possible losers are in the trump suit. There is no reason to delay the drawing of trump.

The correct play with this spade combination is to finesse through East twice. South must be careful to lead the ♠5 from dummy on the first round of trump. On the above lie of the cards, East will follow with his singleton ♠K. South can win the ♠A and use dummy's spades to drive out the ♠Q. Later, the ♠J and ♠10 can be used to draw West's remaining trumps.

Notice that if South makes the mistake of leading the ♠J or ♠9 from dummy on the first round of trump, the contract will fail when East began with a singleton honour. East will cover and West will have 2 certain trump tricks.

If, on the play of the ♠5, East follows small, South should play the ♠10. West may win the trick, but South can win any return and play a second trump from dummy. If East follows low, South should play low from hand, hoping that East began with 3 spades including a top honour.

review.hl: NSJ NS9 NS5 SSA SST SS4 SS3 SS2
NSJ NS9 NS5 SSA SST SS4 SS3 SS2

notes: West leads the ♠Q against 3NT which South wins. There are only 4 top tricks (2 spades, and 2 diamonds). South can establish 4 club tricks once the ♣A is dislodged. The ♥K and ♥Q will also combine for a trick once the ♥A has been knocked out. By that time, however, the defense will have had time to establish and run their spades.

The diamond suit also offers the possibility of extra tricks. After South unblocks the ♦A and ♦K, he might try leading a heart towards the dummy. If West has the ♥A, the ♥Q will be a certain dummy entry. South will be able to take 6 diamond tricks and make at least 9 tricks.

South can actually ensure the contract no matter where the ♥A is placed. After unblocking in diamonds, South should lead the ♥K. If the defense wins the ♥A, the ♥Q will provide an entry to dummy's diamonds.
If South is allowed to hold the ♥K, he can knock out the ♣A and again take 9 tricks (2 spades, the ♥K, 2 diamonds, and 4 clubs).

notes: West leads the ♥K against 4♠. West's lead should be won in dummy with the ♥A as a club shift would not be welcome. It seems tempting to cash the ♦A and ♦K for a heart discard before playing trump.
This is a needless risk, however. The defense may be in a position to ruff the second diamond trick. South still has the ♠A to lose and if clubs are 4-1, the contract will fail.

The chances of being defeated by playing this way are slim, but there is no need to take the risk that the cards will be distributed as above. South should simply play trump at trick 2. After the ♠A is driven out, the defense is welcome to cash a heart trick. South can win any return, draw the outstanding trumps, and discard 1 of his club losers on the dummy's diamond winners. South ends up losing just 1 club trick at the end.
This is a deceptively simple hand. South began with 10 tricks (5 spades, the ♥A, 2 diamonds, and 2 clubs). All that is required is to make sure that one of these tricks is not ruffed.

There are certain losers in spades and clubs. South must avoid losing tricks to both the ♥K and the ♦K. As dummy has only one entry, South must immediately decide which finesse to take.

On the above lie of the cards, a successful heart finesse will not help. If the ♥Q is played from dummy, East will duck. A second heart finesse will leave East with a certain trump trick and South will still have to lose a diamond trick.
Taking a heart finesse requires more than East having the ♥K. East must also have fewer than 4 hearts. Taking the diamond finesse requires only that East hold the ♦K. No additional break is required.

South should therefore finesse diamonds at trick 2. If West follows small, South can drive out the ♥K and easily make the contract. If West wins the ♦K, South still has a small chance that the ♥K is singleton.

South has a near certain way to produce his game-going trick. A low club should be played at trick 2. If West discards, South should win in dummy and hope to develop a ninth trick by finessing twice in diamonds.
If West follows to the first club trick, a low club is played from dummy. If East discards, dummy still has 2 club entries to double finesse in diamonds.

If East follows to the first club trick, the contract is certain as clubs are no worse than 4-1. South can win any return and duck a second round of clubs. South still has stoppers in both majors and dummy's long club will provide trick 9.

notes: In response to his partner's overcall, West leads the ♠Q against 3NT. This lead has guaranteed a spade stopper for South.
There are still only 7 top tricks (1 spade, 4 diamonds, and 2 clubs). South will have to knock out the ♥A to come to 9 tricks.
If East has the ♥A (as is likely from his overcall), South's only hope for the contract is that West began with a singleton ♠Q.
South must duck the opening lead in dummy. If East overtakes with the ♠A, the ♠K and the ♠J both will be stoppers.
If East ducks, West will remain on lead, hopefully with no spades left to play. When East eventually wins the ♥A, South will still have a spade stopper.
If West has the ♥A and a singleton ♠Q, the duck cannot cost.

If West has the ♥A and a doubleton ♠Q, it is again necessary to duck at trick 1. If the ♠K is played from dummy, East will duck in the above layout. When West wins the ♥A, he will have another spade to play to East. By ducking at trick 1, South will be able to exhaust West's spades before the ♥A is knocked out.

notes: West leads the ♠J against 3NT, won by East with the ♠A. East switches to the ♣Q. South has more than enough winners for his contract (2 spades, 2 hearts, and 6 diamonds). His only concern is that the defense may be able to take 4 club tricks to go with their ♠A.

If South covers the ♣Q with the ♣K, the contract might fail. On the above layout, for example, West will win the ♣A and return the suit to East's ♣J. A further club lead from East will sink the contract.

South can ensure the contract by ducking the first round of clubs. Whatever club East continues, South covers as cheaply as possible. West can win this trick, but South's remaining club holding will act as a stopper as long as West is on lead.

notes: West leads the ♥Q against 3NT. There are 8 top tricks (2 spades, 2 hearts, 3 diamonds, and the ♣A). West's heart lead is won by South.
Playing on clubs is too dangerous as an unfavourable break in either clubs or hearts will defeat the contract. South should look towards spades for trick 9.

The spade combination looks like a standard finessing position. It looks like South should cash a top spade in dummy, cross in diamonds, and finesse the ♠J . This plan will work whenever West has the ♠Q and when East has the ♠Q with spades breaking 3-3.

This plan can be improved so that the contract can be made if East has a doubleton ♠Q. After cashing a top spade from dummy, the other top honour should be cashed. If the ♠Q drops, South will succeed immediately.

If, after playing the other top honour, the ♠Q does not appear, South can cross in diamonds and lead towards the ♠J. South still will succeed if West has the ♠Q or if spades are 3-3. The ♣A will act as an entry to the hoped for ninth trick in spades.

notes: West leads the ♥A against 4♠. West cashes 2 heart tricks and continues a third round, South ruffing. South's problem is to avoid the loss of 2 trump tricks.

The normal play with this suit combination is to cash the ♠A and lead low from dummy towards South's holding. On this deal, however, this play is not correct. There are only 17 outstanding high card points. West must have the ♠K for his 1NT opening bid (which shows 15-17 high card points).
South should start by leading the ♠Q from his hand. As long as West began with fewer than 4 spades, South will be able to hold his trump losers to one.

On the above lie of the cards, South can also succeed by passing a low spade through West. This play is not correct as there is room for East to have a singleton ♠J and West to still have a 1NT opening bid. If East is allowed to win a singleton ♠J, West will still have a certain trump trick.

notes: West leads the ♠2 against 7♠. West's opening trump lead is won by South. The only possible loser is the ♦2. If one of the defenders has 5 or more diamonds, South must find a way of disposing of this loser.
South should begin by cashing a second round of trump. If spades prove to be 2-2, the ♦2 can be safely trumped in the dummy.

If a defender discards on the second round of trump, South must proceed with caution. Cashing a third round of trump will leave South dependent on a favourable break in diamonds. Playing on diamonds instead will risk defeat if the defender with the remaining trump also has a singleton diamond.

South should cash his top hearts, discarding a diamond from dummy on the second round. After cashing one top diamond, South can play the ♦2 and trump it in the dummy. As North and South have all of the high trumps, an overruff is not a danger.
South can play a club from dummy and trump it. The last trump can be drawn and South's hand is high.

notes: West leads the ♠K against 4♥. South must lose tricks to the ♥A and ♣A. West's spade lead has created a third certain loser. South must try to avoid losing a diamond trick.
If the ♠A is played at trick 1, the contract will be in trouble. If South tries to knock out the ♥A and ♣A, the defense will play diamonds creating a fourth inescapable loser.

If South instead plays a second round of spades, West will win and switch to diamonds. Dummy will have an established spade winner to take care of South's ♦2, but the dummy cannot be reached without losing the lead.

South does better to let West win at trick one. West will switch to diamonds as before, but South is in control. South can win the ♦A and finesse in spades. The ♠A will take care of South's ♦2 and South's only remaining losers will be the ♥A and the ♣A.

review.hl: ND6 ND5 ND4 ND3 SDA SD2

notes: West leads the ♥10 against 3NT. West's opening lead is overtaken by East with the ♥K. South should win the ♥A as the defense may be able to run the clubs with East on lead.

The contract appears almost certain to make. There are 8 top tricks (3 spades, the ♥A, and 4 diamonds). An additional trick will be available in diamonds unless that suit breaks very badly. The spade suit is another possible source of a ninth trick.

To maximize his chances, South should play the ♠2 to dummy and play a spade back to the ♠A. On the given lie of the cards, South is rewarded. The ♠J drops doubleton leaving South in a position to cash the ♠10. The dummy can be entered in diamonds so that the fourth spade winner can be cashed.

Notice that if the ♦A is played before the spades are tested, South will not be able to take advantage of a doubleton ♠J. The spade suit will be worth 4 tricks, but the blockage in that suit will make only 3 of those tricks available. The contract is still likely to make, but South will have given up on one of his options for trick 9. On the given lie of the cards, the doubleton ♠J is the only option that is working.

notes: West leads the ♣6 against 3♠. West's lead is won by East. East cashes a second top club and returns a third round, West ruffing. West returns a heart, won by South.
The ♠A still must be lost (the bidding marks East with that card). South must be careful not to lose a second trump trick.
If South leads a low spade to dummy's ♠K, he will immediately fail if East has a singleton ♠A as West's remaining trumps will be a certain trick.

Ducking the first round of trump in dummy is not a solution as East may have a doubleton ♠A. Playing the ♠K from dummy will also fail in this case as East will win the ♠A and promote another trump trick with a club return.
The solution is to cross in diamonds and lead the first round of trump from dummy. As long as East has no more than 2 spades he will be powerless to defeat the contract.

NDK NDJ NDT ND9 ND8 SDA SDQ SD2

notes: West leads the ♥A against 5♠ doubled. After winning the first trick he continues the suit at trick 2. It appears that South's only other loser is in diamonds. However, South should be careful. The bidding indicates that West has a very distributional hand and East's double of the final contract suggests he might have all 5 of the outstanding trumps.
If South ruffs at trick 2, he will not be able to prevent the loss of a trump trick to East if East was dealt 5 spades.

South can make the contract on this layout by discarding his diamond loser at trick 2. A diamond trick must be lost in any event and by losing this trick early, South prevents the defense from scoring a trump trick. If a third round of hearts is continued, the ruff can be taken in dummy. South can draw all of the outstanding trumps and easily take the balance.

review.hl: WHQ WHT WH8 WH7 WH6 WH5
ND6 ND5 ND4 ND3 ND2 SDA SD7
NSA NS3 ES8 ES7 ES6 ES5 ES4 SSK SSQ SSJ SST SS9

notes: West leads the ♥10 against 3NT. There are only 7 top tricks (2 spades, 2 hearts, 2 diamonds, and the ♣A). Both spades and clubs offer hope for developing 2 more tricks. South must decide which black suit to play on.

There are two reasons why South should play on spades instead of clubs. First, even if clubs are 3-3, the lead will have to be surrendered twice to develop the suit. The defense may be able to take 2 club tricks and 3 heart tricks.
If spades are 3-3, the lead will have to be surrendered only once. The defense will not be able to establish their hearts in time to defeat the contract.

The other reason to play on spades instead of clubs is the presence of the ♠10 and ♠9. By playing correctly, South can sometimes succeed when spades are 4-2. Playing on clubs will never succeed when clubs are 4-2.

The opening heart lead should be won with the ♥K. South should continue a low spade and, when West follows low, the ♠9 should be played from dummy. If spades are 3-3, there will be no problem. If West began with a doubleton ♠Q or ♠J (or if East began with a doubleton ♠Q ♠J), South will have developed 2 extra tricks in spades.

If East wins this trick and returns a heart, South wins the ♥A. The ♠A will drop West's honour and the ♠K and ♠10 will take care of East's remaining spades. If East allows the ♠9 to hold, South can cash the ♠A, cross in diamonds, and give East a spade trick. South still has a diamond entry to cash the long spade trick.

notes: West leads the ♠8 against 3NT. After South knocks out the ♣A, he will have more than enough tricks (3 hearts, 3 diamonds, and 4 clubs). The only danger is that the defense may be able to take 4 spade tricks after they win the ♣A.

Defenders typically lead the fourth best card from their longest and strongest suit against no trump contracts. West's lead of the ♠8 could be from several possible holdings. The main danger on this deal is that West has a 5 card spade suit along with the ♣A.

If the ♠10 is played from dummy and the defenders' spades are distributed as above, East will win the trick and return the suit. West will drive out the ♠Q and he will be able to cash out his spades upon winning the ♣A.

On the given lie of the cards, South can succeed only by playing low from dummy at trick 1. If East ducks, the blockage in the spade suit will prevent the defense from being able to establish and cash that suit. If East wins at trick 1, dummy's remaining spades will provide two stoppers.

Playing low from dummy at trick 1 does not guarantee the contract. If West has both the ♠A and ♠K, it is necessary to play the ♠Q at trick 1 to block the suit. If West has the ♠A, ♠K, and ♠J it is necessary to play the ♠10 at trick 1. Both of these alternative plays cater to 1 distribution of the outstanding spade honours.
The recommended play of ducking caters to 2 distributions: West holding both the ♠A and ♠J and West holding both the ♠K and ♠J. South should therefore duck in dummy at trick 1.

South seems to have at least 12 top tricks (6 spades, the ♥A, 3 diamonds, and 2 clubs). The only possible danger is that East may be ruffing one of South's diamond tricks.

A low diamond should be played from dummy at trick 1. When East ruffs, South must be careful to unblock the ♦A. South can win any return, draw trump, and take the marked finesse against West's ♦J. Dummy's remaining diamond honours will take care of South's 2 heart losers.

notes: West leads the ♥Q against 6NT. West's lead is won by South. There are 10 top tricks (3 spades, 2 hearts, 3 diamonds, and 2 clubs). Dummy's spade suit is the only possible source of 2 extra tricks.

If spades are 3-2, South can easily take all 13 tricks by cashing the ♠A, ♠K, and ♠Q. If spades are 4-1, there still will be no problem as South can concede a spade trick thereby establishing 2 long card tricks in spades.

South should turn his attention to the possibility that one of the defenders was dealt all 5 spades. South can in fact guard against any distribution of the cards by crossing to the dummy in diamonds and leading a small spade towards the ♠10.

If East has all 5 spades, he has no answer. If East rises with the ♠J, South can win any return in hand. South then unblocks the ♠10 and crosses in diamonds to enjoy 4 more spade tricks. If East ducks the first spade play from dummy, South can win the ♠10 and concede a spade trick to East. Again South will have 5 spade tricks.

If West has all 5 spades, East discards on the first round, and South plays the ♠10. If West wins this trick, South later can take the marked finesse against West's ♠9. If West allows South to win the ♠10, a spade trick can be conceded to West once again establishing a long spade trick in dummy.

notes: West leads the ♦J against 4♥. The opening lead is won by South. The ♠A must be lost and the trump suit is far from solid. South must try to hold his trump losers to 2.
There is a sure way to play the heart combination for no more than 2 losers provided hearts are no worse than 4-1. South begins by cashing the ♥A.

When both defenders follow low (if an honour drops, there is no problem), South should cross in clubs and lead a second round of trump towards the dummy. If West follows low, the play of the ♥Q will guarantee no more than 2 trump losers. If West follows with the ♥K or ♥J, again there will be no problem.
If West discards when a trump is played towards dummy, the ♥Q is played. East will win the ♥K, but South can later lead from dummy towards the ♥10, holding his trump losers to 2.

NCA NC4 NC3 SCK SCQ SC2
NHQ NH6 SHT SH5 SH4 SH3

notes: West leads the ♠K against 3NT. This lead should be ducked by South. This ducking play, when both the ♠A and ♠J are held, is known as the Bath Coup. West cannot continue spades without giving South a second spade trick. If South wins the ♠A, East may later gain the lead in either hearts or diamonds. A spade lead through South's ♠J may put the defense in a position to set the contract.
After the Bath Coup, West cannot profitably continue spades. If he does, South can simply concede a trick to the ♦A and take 9 tricks: (2 spades, 2 hearts, 2 diamonds, and 3 clubs).

West actually shifts to the ♦10. South must be careful not to cover with the ♦J. If South plays low from dummy, East cannot afford to take the ♦A (or else South would have 3 diamond tricks and 9 tricks). East will duck and South wins. South can now duck a heart and make the contract when hearts are 3-2.

If South makes the mistake of playing the ♦J from dummy, East can safely win the ♦A. A spade return from East will spell defeat if West has the 3 card heart holding along with his advertised spade length and strength.

NHA NHK NH4 NH3 NH2 SH7 SH6 SH5

notes: West leads the ♠K against 3NT. This deal looks superficially similar to the last one. It appears at first glance that South should duck, executing the Bath Coup. On this deal, that would not be the correct play. West would shift to hearts and South's ♥A would be driven out eventually. South may have to lose a trick to the ♣Q in order to develop enough tricks. If South misguesses the location of the ♣Q, the defense may take 3 heart tricks in addition to the ♠K and ♣Q.

South can actually guarantee the contract by winning the ♠A at trick 1 and subsequently playing clubs properly. South does not mind losing a club trick as long as he loses that trick to West. West cannot profitably attack spades from his side of the table, but a spade return from East could set the contract.

After winning the ♠A, South should cross to the ♣A and finesse East for the ♣Q. If East has the ♣Q, South will make at least 9 tricks. If West shows out, it may be necessary to finesse East again for the ♣Q.
If West can win the ♣Q, South does not mind. South's ♠J is protected as long as West is on lead and there are 9 easy tricks (the ♠A, the ♥A, 3 diamonds, and 4 clubs).

notes: West leads the ♠K against 4♥. West takes the first 3 spade tricks and switches to a diamond which South wins. South must take the rest of the tricks. If South draws all of the trump, he will go down if diamonds break 4-2 or worse.

South can improve on this plan by drawing only two rounds of trump before testing the diamonds. If diamonds are 3-3, no harm will come of this play as South can draw the last trump and take the balance.

South will also be able to make the contract if diamonds are 4-2 as long as the defender with 4 or more diamonds also has 3 or more hearts. In this case South will be able to ruff his diamond loser in the dummy.
West leads the ♣10 against 4♠. West's lead is won by East with the ♣A. East returns a club.
South must lose a trick to the ♠A as well an eventual trick in diamonds. If South ruffs at trick 2, he will be in trouble if trumps break 4-1. South should try to drive out the ♠A.
If West, for example, has 4 spades including the ♠A, he will hold up the ♠A. When South continues trump, West will duck again.

If South stops playing trump, West may be able to ruff one of South's heart tricks. If South continues trump, West will win the ♠A and play clubs, forcing out South's last trump. The defense will have trump control and the contract will fail.
South can maintain trump control by discarding his diamond loser at trick 2. The diamond loser is inevitable and by giving the defense a second club trick instead, dummy's ♣Q will become a winner.

The club winner prevents the defense from forcing South's trump holding. The third round of clubs is won in dummy and South can now safely draw trump. Even if West holds up until the third round of trump and plays another club, South can ruff, draw West's last trump, and easily take the balance.

NSJ NS7 NS6 SSK SSQ SST SS9 SS8

notes: West leads the ♣7 against 3♠. West's lead is won by East with the ♣K. East cashes the ♣A and continues a third round. South must lose a trick to the ♠A. There is also a certain loser in diamonds.

The defensive carding suggests that West has led from a 4 card club suit headed by the ♣J. As with the previous deal, it seems that South's best play is to discard his certain loser in diamonds in an effort to guard against a possible 4-1 trump break.

West will be allowed to win the ♣J, leaving dummy's ♣10 as a stopper in that suit. There is an additional danger, however. If the spade and club layout is as above, West will lead a fourth club and East will ruff with his singleton trump. South must overruff and West's trump holding will be worth 2 certain tricks.

South should, therefore, ruff at trick 3 and play on trump. If West holds up his ♠A until the third round and plays the ♣J, South can discard his diamond loser. As the defense will have no clubs left to force South's remaining trump, declarer will be able to draw West's last trump after regaining the lead.

ES9 WC9 WSA WS8 WS7 WS6
NSJ NS3 NS2 SSK SSQ SST SS5

notes: West leads the ♠Q against 3NT. West's opening lead drives out South's ♠A. There are only 5 top tricks (the ♠A, 2 hearts, the ♦A, and the ♣A). If West has the ♣K, South can take 4 additional club tricks by finessing in that suit.
It cannot hurt for South to cash the ♦A before playing on clubs. If East has a singleton ♦K, it will be possible to take 4 additional diamond tricks by finessing against West's ♦J and ♦9.
When the ♦K drops, South continues diamonds, covering West's card. After crossing in hearts, South must cash the other heart honour, before finessing again in diamonds.
If East follows with a low diamond on the first round of that suit, South will have to depend on the club finesse.

Notice that East could defeat this plan by dropping the ♦K on the above lie of the cards (among others)! Unless East is an expert player, however, South should take the play of the ♦K at face value and assume it is singleton.

notes: West leads the ♣K against 4♥. South's only top losers are the ♥A and the ♠A, but West's club lead has created two more losers.

North's diamond suit can be used to discard South's club losers, but if diamonds are played before the defenders' trumps are drawn, they will be able to ruff in before South can discard the club losers.

South will also fail if he wins the ♣A and plays hearts immediately. The defense will win the ♥A and cash 2 club tricks and the ♠A. South's best chance is to allow West to win the first trick with the ♣K. South doesn't mind losing 1 club trick and if he loses it at trick 1, the defensive communications may be disrupted.

West will continue clubs, but South wins the ♣A and plays on trump. The defender who wins the ♥A may also have the ♠A and have started with only 2 clubs. Upon winning the ♥A, he will not have a club left nor will he be able to reach his partner's hand in another suit. It is not a very good chance, but it is the best one available. South can win any return, draw trump, and enjoy North's diamond suit.
The hold up play is more common in a no trump contract. As this hand demonstrates, it can be an effective technique in suit contracts as well.
